source.title: Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning in Large Language Models with One Training Example
source.authors: Yiping Wang; Qing Yang; Zhiyuan Zeng; Li-Liang Ren; Lucas Liu; Baolin Peng; Hao Cheng; Xuehai He; Kuan Wang; Jian-Feng Gao; Weizhu Chen; Shuo-Hang Wang; S. Du; Ye-Long Shen

record.tranche_reason: The study measures post-saturation generalization in LLM RLVR and explicitly argues that its mechanism differs from grokking, using loss ablations to distinguish the two.
record.gate_note: The paper reports post-saturation accuracy changes and loss ablations relevant to the claim. It also discusses precision differences between initial checkpoints, but does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause grokking. General benchmark results not bearing on the delayed-generalization behavior or the weight-decay account are omitted.
record.test_reason: New setting (GRPO RLVR fine-tuning of LLMs on one math example) with its own measurements of test accuracy after training accuracy saturates. It also has a weight-decay ablation that the authors use to argue the effect is not grokking. This bears on V4, and only indirectly on V5. It is not a small-algorithmic-dataset study, so it does not bear on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find test performance keeps improving after single-example training accuracy saturates. They say this looks similar to grokking but explicitly do not claim a sudden onset. The loss ablation shows policy gradient loss, not weight decay, drives the gains, which they say distinguishes it from grokking. They credit entropy loss and exploration with sustaining post-saturation improvement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GRPO or PPO reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on LLM math examples, rather than the small-network algorithmic-dataset setup associated with grokking.
record.method_sensitivity: The training example changes the magnitude of improvement; the entropy-loss coefficient and rollout temperature affect post-saturation performance and stability.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-saturation test gains depend on entropy loss / exploration. Without entropy loss, gains are limited beyond step 150; the authors attribute continued gradients to entropy-induced errors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM RLVR, generalization after training saturation is sustained by exploration (entropy) under a policy-gradient signal, not by a norm-reducing regularizer.

record.problems: The authors note that they did not test larger models such as Qwen2.5-32B and mainly studied mathematics rather than other verifiable domains. Reported accuracy changes have no stated error bars or confidence intervals. The study does not test mechanistic circuits or the dataset-size delay relationship.
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark scores and individual example results are not included because they do not independently report the post-saturation behavior or test the weight-decay account. Figure-only values for training curves are not transcribed where the text gives the relevant comparisons.

untested.parts: No small networks on algorithmic datasets; no chance-to-near-perfect jump; no dataset-size versus delay relation.
No circuits, progress measures or memorization-removal analysis.
No variation of initialization scale or weight norm; no non-algorithmic image or molecule data.
Pretraining; non-math domains; models above 7B; a sudden delayed jump (only gradual post-saturation gains measured).
Circuit efficiency, critical dataset size and ungrokking. Weight decay is ablated only at one small coefficient in RLVR.
No comparison of learned algorithms across runs.
The bf16/fp32 checkpoint precision note concerns initial evaluation only. No test of optimizer or softmax numerics as a cause of delay.

missing.what: MATH500 trajectory for π1: 36.0 (step 0), 53.8 (20), 69.8 (60), 70.4 (500), 72.2 (1300), 74.0 (1860). It shows most generalization is immediate, not delayed.
Without entropy loss, 1-shot RLVR shows limited improvement beyond step 150. With entropy loss it gains +2.3 points average, and +0.8 more at temperature 1.0.
Post-saturation test curves for other models (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.2-3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill) are figure-only and not transcribed. Llama degrades before 200 steps.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links removed: LLM math RLVR is not a small algorithmic dataset. The V5 challenge was downgraded to limits_scope: the ablation shows weight decay is irrelevant in a phenomenon the authors themselves argue is not grokking, and the measure is best-checkpoint accuracy, not the delay. Weight decay was 0.01 at LR 1e-6 over at most 2000 steps, a weak regularizer. No error bars or seeds are reported. Tranche changed to T3: a new setting, with the anti-grokking argument secondary.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses LLMs trained by RLVR on math examples, not small networks trained on modular-arithmetic-style algorithmic datasets. It does not test a test-accuracy rise from chance to near-perfect or whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
No circuit formation, memorizing-component removal, Fourier algorithm, or continuous mechanistic progress measure is tested.
The study does not test non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule datasets, nor vary initialization scale or weight norm to switch delayed generalization on or off.
The study tests RLVR fine-tuning of LLMs on mathematical reasoning data, not pretraining or fine-tuning on broad realistic non-mathematical data or larger models such as 32B.
The study ablates weight decay in its RLVR setting but does not measure circuit efficiency, low-norm circuits, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.

The study discusses a numerical-precision difference between checkpoints but does not test whether optimizer instability or softmax floating-point limits produce grokking or make it disappear when controlled.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: base model; trained with GRPO RLVR
rows.operation_detail: Measured evaluation accuracy during 1-shot RLVR training on π1 after training accuracy had saturated.
rows.measure: Change in average test performance after training accuracy saturation
rows.value: 3.4% average improvement from step 100 to step 1540
rows.note: The text reports continued improvement, but does not describe a jump to near-perfect test accuracy.
rows.check: LLM RLVR on math is not a small algorithmic dataset, so V1 is dropped. Test average rises 3.4 points after saturation, but most of the gain came before saturation. Footnote 5 says the authors do not claim a sudden onset, so this is a modest gradual creep, not a delayed jump.

rows.value: 9.9% average improvement from step 500 to step 2000
rows.note: The reported continued improvement is post-saturation, but does not establish the chance-to-near-perfect pattern in V1.
rows.check: V1 dropped (not an algorithmic dataset). Test average rises 9.9 points from step 500 to 2000 after saturation before step 100. The rise is gradual; the authors liken the curve to double descent rather than a sudden jump.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: base model; trained with GRPO RLVR
rows.operation_detail: Measured test performance after the authors report overfitting to the single training example.

conditions.value: authors describe the training response as significantly overfit

rows.note: The paper says the test response remained normal and describes test performance as strong after training-example overfitting; 74% is not near-perfect.
rows.check: A single test value (74% MATH500 at step 1860) cannot show delayed generalization. Table 15 shows MATH500 already at 69.8 by step 60 and 70.4 at step 500. Baseline should be base 36.0 or the pre-overfit checkpoint.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: base model; trained with GRPO RLVR
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the loss to use policy gradient loss without weight decay, KL loss, or entropy loss.
rows.note: The authors say this result is close to full-loss training and attribute the main improvement to policy gradient loss.
rows.check: Measures the policy-gradient contribution to best MATH500 accuracy, not any weight-decay or low-norm effect. It is a comparator for r6, not a V5 result.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: base model; trained with GRPO RLVR
rows.operation_detail: Added weight decay and KL loss to policy gradient loss.

conditions.value: policy gradient + weight decay + KL loss

rows.note: The authors describe adding weight decay and KL loss as having no significant impact.
rows.check: Adding weight decay (0.01, LR 1e-6) to PG-only gives 71.4 vs 71.8; the authors call this no significant impact. The measure is best-checkpoint accuracy, not the delay itself. Single run, no error bars.

source_check.correct: Table 5 row 2: policy-gradient loss alone, 71.8% MATH500. Row 3: policy-gradient loss plus weight decay, without KL or entropy loss, 71.4%. Row 4: policy-gradient loss plus weight decay and KL loss, 70.8%. Results are best-checkpoint performance on each benchmark separately. State for V5: cannot_determine; this endpoint-accuracy ablation does not measure circuit efficiency, critical dataset size, ungrokking, or a change in generalization timing.
source_check.locator_found: Table 5 caption and rows 2–4; Section 4.1; Appendix B.4.
source_check.problem: The 71.4% value belongs to the weight-decay-only addition, and negligible endpoint-accuracy change cannot establish absence of V5's mechanism.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
rows.stage_stated: base model; trained with GRPO RLVR
rows.operation_detail: Trained using weight decay and KL loss without policy gradient loss.
rows.note: The authors say weight decay and KL alone have little influence on model performance.
rows.check: Weight decay plus KL without any task loss cannot be expected to produce generalization under V5 either, so this row cannot test the efficiency account.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B

rows.operation_detail: Used the full loss with policy gradient, weight decay, KL loss, and entropy loss.

conditions.value: policy gradient + weight decay + KL loss + entropy loss

rows.note: The authors compare this with policy-gradient-only training and say entropy loss further improves results.
rows.check: Full-loss result showing the entropy-loss contribution. It bears on no version's weight-decay mechanism and serves as the ablation reference.

relationships.reason: Test accuracy keeps rising after training saturates (r1, r2), but by only 3.4–9.9 points and gradually. Most of the gain arrives before saturation (Table 15, from text), so it is not a delayed jump.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy rose gradually by 3.4–9.9 points after training saturated, with most gains occurring before saturation.

source_check.reason: r1 and r2 establish continued post-saturation improvement without establishing a sudden delayed transition. The label is defensible, but its assertion that most improvement preceded saturation for both runs is not established by Table 15.

relationships.reason: Training accuracy never saturated and test performance plateaued after step 1000, so no post-saturation generalization occurs with the full dataset (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy never saturated on the 1.2k-example dataset, while test performance plateaued after step 1000.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r3 supplies a contrasting tested condition: training remains unsaturated after 2000 steps, and test performance shows no significant improvement after step 1000. The post-saturation pattern is therefore conditional on the training setup within the observed runs.

relationships.reason: Weight decay changes best MATH500 by -0.4 points (r6). The post-saturation gains in this LLM setting do not depend on a weight-decay bias. The study does not test V5 in its original grokking setting.
relationships.display_finding: Adding weight decay reduced best MATH500 accuracy by 0.4 points, while post-saturation gains occurred without it.

relation.reason: Its training and test trajectories directly bear on V4, and it explicitly compares the observed phenomenon with grokking.

tranche.reason: The study measures post-saturation generalization in a new setting: RLVR fine-tuning of pretrained LLMs on individual math examples.

source_check.notes: The authors distinguish post-saturation generalization from grokking and leave its mechanism unresolved. Their weight-decay interpretation should not be promoted into a direct test of the complete V5 efficiency account.

statements.correction: Section 3.2.2: training saturates before step 100 for both examples; π1 gains 3.4% average performance from steps 100–1540; π13 gains 9.9% from steps 500–2000. Footnote 5: sudden onset is not emphasized. Table 15: MATH500 evaluation under Qwen-Eval and QwQ-32B, rather than six-benchmark averages for both runs.
statements.problem: The post-saturation gains are correct, but Table 15 does not establish that most six-benchmark improvement occurred before saturation for both examples; it reports MATH500 judge comparisons.
